Introduction

1.      Let X be the Poincaré half-plane

                    X = {z ∈ ℂ | Im(z) > 0}.

The group SL(2, ℝ) acts on X by homographic transformations

                            az+b
                    z ↦  ─────.
                            cz+d

If Γ is a subgroup of SL(2, ℤ) defined by congruence conditions, the Riemann
surface X/Γ is the complement of a finite set of points ("at infinity") in a
compact Riemann surface. It is therefore an algebraic curve. Its points are in
bijective correspondence with the isomorphism classes of elliptic curves equipped
with a "level structure" of a suitable kind. It is known from this interpretation
that it admits as a field of definition a subfield of a cyclotomic field. In this
article, we study the structure at infinity and the reduction modulo p of X/Γ.

Let us concentrate on the case in which Γ is the subgroup of SL(2, ℤ) formed
by the matrices congruent modulo n to the identity matrix. Suppose that n ≥ 3, in
which case Γ acts on X without a fixed point.

For z ∈ X, let E_z denote the quotient of ℂ by the lattice ℤ + ℤz. The
addition law on ℂ descends to the quotient and equips E_z with the structure of an
elliptic curve (= an abelian variety of dimension one). The elliptic curves E_z and
E_z′ are isomorphic if and only if z and z′ are conjugate under SL(2, ℤ).
The kernel E(z)_n of multiplication by n on E(z) is the image of (1/n)(ℤ + ℤz);
we shall denote by α(z) the isomorphism

        E(z)_n  ≃  (ℤ/nℤ)^2 : (a+bz)/n ↦ (a,b).
translation_notes: “Transformations homographiques” is rendered “homographic transformations”; formulas are unchanged.

text:
For the pairs (E(z),α(z)) and (E(z′),α(z′)) to be isomorphic, it is necessary and
sufficient that z and z′ be conjugate under Γ.

For every elliptic curve E over an algebraically closed field k of
characteristic p not dividing n, the group E_n is equipped with a nondegenerate
alternating form e_n with values in the nth roots of unity in k. A level-n
structure on E is an isomorphism α:E_n ≃ (ℤ/n)^2.
If α is a level-n structure, we shall denote by ζ(α) the primitive nth root
of unity

        ζ(α) = e_n(α^−1((1,0)), α^−1((0,1))).

Put k = ℂ, and set ζ_n = exp(2πi/n). A pair (E,α) is isomorphic to a pair
(E(z),α(z)) (z ∈ X) if and only if

        ζ(α) = ζ_n

(or ζ_n^−1, according to the sign convention used in the definition of e_n).

2.      The foregoing generalizes to families of elliptic curves parametrized by a
scheme S. One finds that X/Γ represents the following functor F_n on schemes over
ℂ: F_n(T) is the set of isomorphism classes of algebraic families, parametrized by
T, of elliptic curves E equipped with a level-n structure such that ζ(α) = ζ_n.

The definition of F_n(T) remains meaningful when T is merely assumed to be a
scheme over ℤ[ζ_n, 1/n]. Igusa proved in [11] that the resulting functor F_n is
representable by a scheme M_n^∘[1/n] over ℤ[ζ_n,1/n]. Igusa's method is as follows.

text:
a) If M_n^∘[1/n] exists, then M_nm^∘[1/nm] exists. If E is an elliptic curve
over an algebraically closed field, multiplication by m induces an isomorphism of
E_nm/nE_nm with E_n; a level-nm structure α:E_nm ≃ (ℤ/nm)^2 thereby defines, by
reduction modulo n, a level-n structure. This carries over to an arbitrary base
scheme and defines a morphism of functors F_nm → F_n. This morphism is relatively
representable. It makes M_nm^∘[1/nm] an unramified Galois covering, with group
Ker(SL(2, ℤ/nm) → SL(2, ℤ/n)), of

        M_n^∘[1/nm] ⊗_{ℤ[ζ_n]} ℤ[ζ_nm]

(⊗ denotes an extension of scalars).

b) If M_nm^∘[1/nm] exists, M_n^∘[1/nm] exists. One obtains M_n^∘[1/nm] by passing to
the quotient.

c) M_3^∘[1/3] and M_4^∘[1/4] exist. Explicitly, one has

        M_3^∘[1/3] = Spec(ℤ[ζ_3,1/3,μ,(μ^3−1)^−1]),

with universal elliptic curve the plane cubic with equation

        X^3 + Y^3 + Z^3 = 3μ XYZ.

The zero section is (1,−1,0), and the basis of the group of points of order 3 is
((−1,0,1), (−1,ζ_3,0)).

At level 4, one has

        M_4^∘[1/4] = Spec(ℤ[i,1/2,σ,(σ(σ^4−1))^−1]),

where i = ζ_4, with universal elliptic curve the plane cubic whose nonhomogeneous
equation is

        y^2 = x(x−1)(x−λ),  where

        λ = (1/4)(σ + 1/σ)^2.

The zero section is the point at infinity, and the basis (r,s) of the group of points

of order 4 is given by

        r = (1/2(σ + 1/σ), i(σ²+1)(σ−1)²/(4·σ²))

        s = (−i/2(σ − 1/σ) + 1, −(σ²−1)(σ+1)²/(4·σ²)).

The formulas above for M_4^∘[1/4] are copied from Shioda [31]. Igusa used not
M_4^∘[1/4], but the moduli scheme of elliptic curves equipped with a structure
intermediate between a level-4 structure and a level-2 structure.

d) M_n^∘[1/n] is obtained by gluing M_n^∘[1/3n] and M_n^∘[1/4n].

3.      The Riemann surface X/Γ is noncompact. Geometrically, this fact translates as
follows: if E_η is an elliptic curve equipped with a level-n structure over ℂ((T)),
it may happen that the minimal model of E_η over ℂ[[T]] has bad reduction. In that
case, the special fiber E'_o of the Néron model E' of E_η over ℂ[[T]] is
isomorphic to ℂ*×ℤ/kn for a suitable k. Let E_o be the subgroup of E'_o that is
the union of the components of E'_o whose order in π_o(E'_o) divides n. This
subgroup is isomorphic to ℂ*×ℤ/n. It has the following advantage over E'_o: after
extending scalars from ℂ((T)) to ℂ((T^{1/ℓ})), the number of connected components
of E'_o is multiplied by ℓ, while E_o remains unchanged.

By specialization, the alternating form e_n defines an alternating form, again
denoted e_n, on (E_o)_n. By specialization, the level-n structure α defines

        α_o : (E_o)_n ≃ (ℤ/n)²,

and

        ζ(α_o) = e_n(α^−1((1,0)), α^−1((0,1))) = ζ_n.

This discussion suggests that the points at infinity of X/Γ correspond

to the isomorphism classes of systems (E_o,e_n,α_n) as above. This is indeed
the case.

In the text, we refine this modular interpretation of the set of points at infinity
of X/Γ into a modular interpretation of the projective curve X/Γ̄, the compactification
of X/Γ. Here is the principle.

For E_η over ℂ((T)) as above, the special fiber Ē'_o of the minimal model Ē' of
E_η over ℂ[[T]] is a cycle of kn projective lines:

        [cycle of kn projective lines: see authority asset P0008-A01]

Let Ē be obtained from Ē' by contracting to a point the irreducible components of
Ē'_o whose order does not divide n. The special fiber Ē_o of Ē is a cycle of n
projective lines meeting transversely, and is a compactification of E_o (E_o
identifies with the smooth locus Ē_o^reg of Ē_o). By specialization, + and α define
a group law on the smooth locus Ē_o^reg of Ē_o, an action of Ē_o^reg on Ē_o, and
an isomorphism

        α_o : (Ē_o^reg)_n ≃ (ℤ/n)².

Let T be a scheme of finite type over ℂ. Inspired by the remarks above, we define
a generalized elliptic curve over T, equipped with a level-n structure α such that
ζ(α) = ζ_n, as consisting of:

a) a proper flat morphism p : E → T;

b) a commutative group-scheme structure on the open subset E^reg of E where p is
smooth; addition is assumed to extend to an action

        + : E^reg ×_T E → E;

The authority distinguishes the special fiber Ē'_o from the minimal model Ē'.

Artin representability discussion and modular curve conclusion

text:
c) an isomorphism of group schemes

        (E^reg)_n ≃ (ℤ/n)²_T.

The geometric fibers of p are assumed either to be elliptic curves equipped with a
level-n structure such that ζ(α) = ζ_n, or to be isomorphic to one of the systems
(Ē_o,α_o) constructed above.

We prove that the curve X/Γ̄ represents the following functor F̄_n on schemes of finite
type over ℂ. F̄_n(T) is the set of isomorphism classes of generalized elliptic curves
E over T, equipped with a level-n structure α such that ζ(α) = ζ_n.

To make the definition of generalized elliptic curves viable, we make intensive use
of Grothendieck techniques (base-change theorems (EGA III) and duality ([10]) in
coherent-sheaf cohomology). These techniques provide a systematic means of reducing
relative statements concerning schemes over a base scheme S to the case in which S
is the spectrum of an algebraically closed field.

To prove that the functor F̄_n is representable, we use the general criterion of M.
Artin [3]. Verifying the hypotheses of this criterion presents the following delicate
point. Datum b) in the definition of a generalized elliptic curve is a morphism of
schemes over T

        + : E^reg ×_T E → E,

whose source E^reg ×_T E is not necessarily proper over T. This forces us to
prove the effective prorepresentability of F_n by an indirect route, since
Grothendieck's existence theorem is not directly applicable.

Chapters II and III and §1 of IV contain the tools required to overcome these
difficulties. Above, we worked over ℂ. In the text, we work over ℤ or ℤ[ζ_n], as
appropriate, and obtain a curve M_n[1/n], projective and smooth over ℤ[ζ_n,1/n],
solving a moduli problem, and such that X/Γ̄ is obtained from it by extension of
scalars to ℂ.
translation_notes: Barred F_n is retained for the compactified functor; plain F_n is retained in the effective-prorepresentability sentence.

4.      To speak of the "reduction mod p of X/Γ̄" presupposes the choice of a
model M_n of X/Γ̄ over ℤ[ζ_n]. The definition of M_n given in the text is equivalent
to the following: M_n is the normalization of the j-line (the projective line over
ℤ[ζ_n], to which M_n maps by the "modular invariant of the universal elliptic
curve" map) in the function field of M_n^∘[1/n]. Also let M_n^∘ be the affine curve
whose coordinate ring is the normalization of ℤ[ζ_n][j] in the coordinate ring of
M_n^∘. It is shown in the text that

        M_n[1/n] = M_n ⊗_{ℤ[ζ_n]} ℤ[ζ_n,1/n]     and

        M_n^∘[1/n] = M_n^∘ ⊗_{ℤ[ζ_n]} ℤ[ζ_n,1/n].

We prove the following results:

a) The modular curve M_n is projective over ℤ[ζ_n], and smooth away from a finite
set of points of M_n^∘, namely the supersingular points whose characteristic divides
n.

b) There exists a finite family of points f_i of M_n with values in ℤ[ζ_n] (= sections
of the scheme morphism M_n → Spec(ℤ[ζ_n])), such that

b1) the sections f_i are disjoint (= the points f_i are incongruent modulo every
prime ideal of ℤ[ζ_n]);

b2) M_n^∘ is the complement in M_n of the union of the "sections at infinity" f_i.

c) Let 𝔭 be a prime ideal of ℤ[ζ_n] dividing the prime factor p of n. We determine
the set of irreducible components of the reduction of M_n modulo 𝔭. To describe the
result, we suppose that n is the product of two relatively prime integers ≥ 3, n'
and n''. Under this hypothesis, M_n[1/n'] is the normalization in M_n^∘[1/n] of the
scheme M_{n'}[1/n'], for which we know a modular interpretation. The pullbacks to
M_{n'}^∘[1/n'] and M_{n''}^∘[1/n''] of the

universal elliptic curves over M_{n'}^∘[1/n'] and M_{n''}^∘[1/n''] glue together
and furnish a universal elliptic curve E over M_n^∘. The level structure

        α : E_n ≃ (ℤ/n)²

over M_n^∘[1/n] extends to a morphism of group schemes over M_n^∘,

        α^−1 : (ℤ/n)² → E_n.

The p-primary component of α^−1 is a morphism

        β(p) : (ℤ/p^k)² → E_{p^k}.

The supersingular points of characteristic p of M_𝔭 (p|n) are those at which
β(p) is zero. The irreducible components of the reduction of M_n modulo 𝔭 are in
bijective correspondence with the cyclic subgroups of order p^k of (ℤ/p^k)² (the
points of ℙ¹(ℤ/p^k)): at the nonsupersingular points of the component indexed by
A ⊂ (ℤ/p^k)², the kernel of β(p) is A. We prove that these irreducible components
are unibranch, and that any two of them meet at every supersingular point.

The irreducible components of the reduction of M_n modulo p had been determined by
Pjateckii-Shapiro (see his article in this volume). Unfortunately, he works with
PGL(2) rather than GL(2), so that his results are more tangled than ours.

Under the same hypothesis on n as above, one of us (P. Deligne) recently proved that
these irreducible components are in fact smooth, and that M_n is a regular scheme.

To study M_n, the first step is to cover by open subsets having a modular
interpretation the open subset M_n^h of M_n obtained by removing the supersingular
points whose characteristic divides n. This is achieved by studying the moduli
scheme classifying elliptic curves equipped with an isomorphism

α : E_n ≃ μ_n × ℤ/n.

A modular interpretation makes it possible

a) to determine the set of points of M_n over an algebraically closed field;

b) to prove the smoothness of M_n^h over ℤ[ζ_n]. It remains, and this is the most
delicate point, to study the supersingular points.

5.      It is no doubt possible to study the structure of M_n at infinity by rigid-
analytic methods, using the theory of the Tate curve, without first giving the
points at infinity a modular description. Such an approach may even be the only
practicable one for studying the boundary of higher-dimensional moduli schemes. It
has often served us as a heuristic guide (see below). However, to make it precise,
it requires rigid-analytic preliminaries that we wished to avoid.

This explains why the Tate curve appears only in the final chapter, Chapter VII.
We use it to deduce properties at finite distance of the M_n, and of their reduction
modulo p, from results on the Fourier-series expansions of modular forms. In
particular, we prove the following results.

− The graded algebra of modular forms on X/Γ whose expansions at all cusps have
coefficients in ℤ[ζ_n] is a finitely generated algebra over ℤ[ζ_n].

− If the prime ideal 𝔭 of ℤ[ζ_n] does not divide n, and if at one cusp the
Fourier-series expansion of a modular form φ on X/Γ has coefficients in ℚ[ζ_n] and
is 𝔭-integral, then the expansion of φ at the other cusps has the same properties.

Fragmentary indications are also given for the case where 𝔭 divides n.
translation_notes: The source's underlined phrase ‘à distance finie’ is rendered ‘at finite distance’.
Plain X/Γ is retained in the Fourier-expansion statements.

assets.caption: Tate-curve principles and Serre–Tate local theory
Quaternionic modular curve and local-structure comparison

6.      Our heuristic use of the Tate curve rests on the following principles.

a) With the aid of the Tate curve, one can guess or prove what happens in a
neighborhood of infinity.

b) Outside the supersingular points, the situation is everywhere the same, and in
particular the same as in a neighborhood of infinity.

        To these principles is added the following one.

c) Geometrically, i.e. after extension of scalars (or of the residue field) to 𝔽̄_p,
the situation is the same at the various supersingular points of characteristic p.

        The local (formal) theory of M_n in a neighborhood of the geometric points
corresponding to an elliptic curve E over 𝔽̄_p is governed by the p-divisible group

        D_p(E) = ⋃ E_{p^n},

that is, essentially, by the completed formal group of E at the origin. This follows
from the Serre–Tate theorem, according to which E and this p-divisible group have
the same deformation theory. Principles b) and c) follow from it, since this
p-divisible group depends, up to isomorphism, only on whether E is ordinary or
supersingular.

7.      Let H be an indefinite quaternion algebra, of discriminant D, over ℚ, and
let Δ be a congruence subgroup of the group of units of H. The group Δ is a discrete
subgroup of SL(2,ℝ) with compact quotient. The complete curve X/Δ parametrizes
abelian varieties A of dimension 2, equipped with a homomorphism from an order of H
into End(A) ("false elliptic curves," in Serre's terminology). Our methods apply to
the study of X/Δ and of its reduction modulo p, provided that p is prime to D.

        The following remarks even make it possible to deduce, from theorems for
M_n, theorems on the local structure of X/Δ.
translation_notes: ‘In a neighborhood of infinity’ literally renders au voisinage de l'infini.
Soit essentiellement is retained as ‘that is, essentially’ without strengthening the relationship.

        D_p A) = e·D_p(A) ⊕ (1−e)D_p(A).

The abelian scheme A, equipped with μ, and the p-divisible group eD_p(A), have the
same deformation theory.

e) the p-divisible group eD_p(A) is isomorphic to D_p(E) for an elliptic curve E

        The reduction modulo p of X/Δ was studied by Morita. He also obtains results
in the much more difficult case where p|D.

8.      In the literature on moduli schemes, the language of Weil's Foundations is
sometimes used. According as one uses this language or Grothendieck's, emphasis is
placed on one of the following two views of what a scheme X over a number field K is.

a) It is a scheme X, equipped with a morphism X → Spec(K). This is the view that
predominates in our notation.

b) It is a scheme X̄ over the algebraic closure K̄ of K, which is defined over K.
This view shows through in the proof technique that consists in reducing a statement
concerning an S-scheme X to a statement concerning its geometric fibers X_s̄,
obtained by extension of scalars from S to an algebraically closed field k(s̄).

        The "restriction of scalars à la Grothendieck" from K to ℚ takes on a very
different appearance according to the view adopted.

a) To the K-scheme X one associates the ℚ-scheme defined by X and the composite
morphism X → Spec(K) → Spec(ℚ). It is not distinguished from X in the notation. A
scheme is first of all a ℚ-scheme; if it is a K-scheme, it is equipped with a
ℚ-morphism X → Spec(K).

b) Let I be the set of embeddings of K into ℚ̄. For σ ∈ I, set

represents the functor of isomorphism classes of elliptic curves E/T, equipped with
an isomorphism

        α : E_n ≃ (ℤ/n)².

Such a pair (E,α) defines (by the theory of the alternating form e_n) a primitive
n-th root of unity ζ(α) over T, hence a morphism of schemes

        (E,α) ↦ ζ(α) : M_n^∘[1/n] → Spec(ℤ[ζ_n,1/n]).

        Viewed as a ℤ[ζ_n,1/n]-scheme, M_n^∘[1/n] classifies the (E,α)/T, with T
a ℤ[ζ_n,1/n]-scheme, such that ζ(α) = ζ_n.

whereas, if one puts X^± = ℂ − ℝ,

is the sum of φ(n) copies of X/Γ.

9.      An elliptic curve over an algebraically closed field k has one or more
nontrivial automorphisms. This rules out representability of the functor that assigns
to a scheme T the set of isomorphism classes of elliptic curves E over T: it is not
even a sheaf. This can be remedied in two ways.

a) Systematically impose additional level structures that eliminate these
automorphisms. This is what we have done in this introduction.

b) Use the language of algebraic stacks, for which we refer to [8] and [17].
This is what we do in the text, for the following reasons.

1. Imposing an additional level structure modifies the behavior at infinity of the
objects studied (M_{n̄m} ramifies over M_n along infinity).

2. The calculations and proofs become simpler when one does not have to concern
oneself with troublesome additional structures.

        In Chapter VI, from our results on modular stacks we deduce results on the
coarse moduli schemes (= coarse modular schemes) usually considered.

10.     We refer to the table of contents and to the introductions of the various

text:
Notations

The work is divided into chapters; each chapter is divided into sections. Internal
references within a single chapter do not mention the number of that chapter.

        We shall freely use the definitions and notation of the theory of algebraic
stacks as set out in [8] §4. However, contrary to the terminology of loc. cit., a
morphism of categories fibered in groupoids

        φ : 𝔐_1 → 𝔐_2

will be called representable if, for every morphism x : X → 𝔐_2 from a scheme X to
𝔐_2, the fiber product 𝔐_1 ×_{𝔐_2} X is an algebraic space.

        A group scheme G over a scheme S is sometimes called an S-group. The
subgroup scheme that is the kernel of multiplication by n in G is denoted by G_n.

        Let X be an S-scheme. If T is an S-scheme, we denote by X_T the fiber
product X ×_S T. If S = Spec(A) and T = Spec(B), X_B, or X ⊗_A B, have the same
meaning. For n ∈ ℕ, we set X[1/n] = X ⊗_ℤ ℤ[1/n].

        We set ζ_n = exp(2πi/n).

        For the principles governing our notation for modular stacks, we refer to
§0 of Chapter III.

text:
I Preliminaries

        This chapter gathers well-known results of which we shall have occasion to
make use. The reader is invited to consult it only as needed.

1. Curve schemes.

1.0.     In this section, a curve scheme over a scheme S means a proper and flat
morphism of finite presentation, of relative dimension at most 1.

1.1.     If C/S is a curve scheme over S, the Euler–Poincaré characteristic
χ(𝒪_{C_s}) of the fibers is locally constant (EGA III, 7.9.). The arithmetic genus
g_s of C_s is defined by

        1 − g_s = χ(C_s,𝒪_{C_s}).

If the Euler–Poincaré characteristic of the fibers is constant with value 1 − g,
C|S is called a curve scheme of genus g, or simply a curve of genus g over S.

1.2.     A morphism p : X → S is said to be Cohen–Macaulay if it is flat and of
finite presentation and its (geometric) fibers are Cohen–Macaulay schemes.

        A Cohen–Macaulay curve scheme over S is a curve scheme p : C → S that is
Cohen–Macaulay and whose geometric fibers are purely of dimension one. Likewise,
when we speak of smooth, reduced, or integral curves, "purely of dimension one"
will be understood.

        For S = Spec(A), we shall speak interchangeably of curves over S and curves
over A.
translation_notes: ‘Curve scheme’ consistently renders the defined term schéma en courbes.
The typography C|S is deliberately preserved exactly and is not normalized to C/S.
The parenthetical ‘(geometric)’ and pure-dimension qualification retain their source scope.

2. Duality in the cohomology of coherent sheaves.

2.1.     We propose to recall what Grothendieck duality theory provides for a
morphism p : X → S when

a) p is Cohen–Macaulay, purely of relative dimension d; and

b) S is Noetherian.

In the applications we have in view, we could always reduce to the case in which p
is moreover quasi-projective.

        The relative dualizing complex Rp^!𝒪_S [10] has only one nonzero cohomology
sheaf, that of degree −d; it is the sheaf of regular differentials

(2.1.1.)        ω_{X/S} = ℋ^{−d}(Rp^!𝒪_S)

([10] V. 9.7.). This sheaf is flat over S. Its formation commutes with every base
change S' → S and with étale localization on X (see [10] or [34]).

2.2.     If p is moreover proper, one defines a "trace" morphism

(2.2.1)         Tr : R^d p_*(ω_{X/S}) → 𝒪_S

whose formation is compatible with every base change. The duality theorem asserts
that, for every bounded complex of coherent sheaves K, the arrow deduced from Tr,

(2.2.2.)        Rp_* R Hom_{𝒪_X}(K,ω_{X/S})[−d] ≃ R Hom_{𝒪_S}(Rp_*K,𝒪_S),

is an isomorphism.

R^i p_*(F) are locally free, (2.2.2.) becomes

(where ∨ denotes the dual of an 𝒪_X-module, respectively of an 𝒪_S-module).

        ω_{X/S} is an invertible sheaf if and only if p is Gorenstein [10].

        For S not necessarily Noetherian, one defines ω_{X/S} and Tr by passage to
the limit; for K a bounded complex of locally free sheaves, (2.2.2.) remains valid
and is proved by passage to the limit.

        When S is the spectrum of a field k, ω_{X/S} will also be denoted ω_{X/k},
or simply ω_X.

2.3.     Let X be a reduced curve over an algebraically closed field k, and let
π : X̃ → X be the normalization of X. The sheaf ω_X is identified with the following
subsheaf of the direct image under π of the sheaf of meromorphic differentials on
X. The sections of ω_X over U are the meromorphic differentials ω on π^{−1}(U) such
that, for every P ∈ U and every f ∈ 𝒪_{X,P},

        ∑_{R↦P} Res_R(f·ω) = 0.

If the only singularities of X are ordinary double points P_i, and
π^{−1}(P_i) = {P'_i,P''_i}, the regular differentials on X are identified with the
meromorphic differential forms ω on X̃ that are regular away from P'_i,P''_i, have
at worst a simple pole at P'_i and P''_i, and satisfy

        Res_{P'_i}(ω) + Res_{P''_i}(ω) = 0

([27], Chapter IV).

text:
3. Review of the Picard functor.

3.1.     Let p : X → S be a proper flat morphism of finite presentation. The
relative Picard functor of X over S, denoted Pic_{X/S}, is the fppf sheaf associated
with the presheaf

(3.1.1)         S' ↦ Pic(X ×_S S') = the group of isomorphism classes of invertible
                sheaves on X ×_S S'.

The canonical morphism Pic(X)/Pic(S) → Pic_{X/S}(S) is injective if
p_*𝒪_X = 𝒪_S. It is bijective if, in addition, p has a section (TDTE V.2.4.).

3.2.     One says that p is cohomologically flat in dimension 0 (EGA III, 7.),
or simply cohomologically flat, if the formation of p_*𝒪_X commutes with every base
change S' → S. A fundamental theorem of M. Artin asserts that, if p is proper, flat
of finite presentation, and cohomologically flat, then Pic_{X/S} is representable by
an algebraic space locally of finite presentation over S ([2] Thm. 7.3). If, in
addition, p : X → S is a curve scheme, Pic_{X/S} is smooth over S.

        If Pic_{X/S} is representable by an algebraic space, Pic^o_{X/S} denotes the
subfunctor in groups of Pic_{X/S} that is the neutral component of Pic_{X/S}. If
p : X → S is a curve scheme, it is representable by an algebraic space.

3.3.     Let C be a proper curve over a field k. If ℒ is an invertible sheaf on C,
its degree deg_C(ℒ) is defined by the Riemann–Roch formula

(3.3.1)         χ(ℒ) = deg_C(ℒ) + χ(𝒪_C).

Then (cf. [15])

(3.3.2)         deg_C(ℒ_1 ⊗ ℒ_2) = deg_C(ℒ_1) + deg_C(ℒ_1).

6. Division points of elliptic curves.

        Let E be an elliptic curve (an abelian variety of dimension one) over an algebraically closed field k.

        For every integer n ≥ 1, the group scheme E_n, the kernel of multiplication by n, is known to be the spectrum of a Hopf algebra of dimension n^2 over k. If n is invertible in k, then E_n ≃ (ℤ/n)^2.

        If k has characteristic p > 0, the kernel of the Frobenius morphism F : E → E^(p) has rank p. It is isomorphic to μ_p or to α_p. If it is isomorphic to μ_p, E is said to be ordinary, and E_n ≃ ℤ/n × μ_n. Otherwise E is said to be supersingular.

        In the exact sequence

        0 → Ker(F) → E_p → E_p/Ker(F) → 0,

the two extreme terms are Cartier dual. If E is supersingular, E_p is therefore isomorphic to α_{p^2}, the unique nontrivial extension killed by p of α_p by α_p.

        The supersingular elliptic curves over k are all isogenous and form a finite number of isomorphism classes (cf. [32]).

7. Review of commutative algebra.

        We shall often use the following results from commutative algebra; for their proofs we refer to EGA.

(7.1)     Let f : X → Y be a morphism of finite type between Noetherian schemes. If Y is Cohen–Macaulay and f is flat, then X is Cohen–Macaulay if and only if the fibers of f are. For example, if Y is Cohen–Macaulay and f is quasi-finite and flat, then X is Cohen–Macaulay.

        If Y is regular, X is Cohen–Macaulay, and at the point x ∈ X with image y ∈ Y one has

(7.1 1)        dim(𝒪_{X,x}) = dim(𝒪_{Y,y}) + dim(𝒪_{X,x} ⊗_{𝒪_{Y,y}} k(y)),

then f is flat at x. Condition (7.1.1) is satisfied if f is quasi-finite and dominant and X is irreducible.

        EGA IV 6.3.5 and EGA IV 6.1.5.

(7.2)     Let Y be Noetherian of dimension two. For Y to be normal, it is necessary and sufficient that Y be Cohen–Macaulay and regular except at points of codimension two.

        EGA IV. 5.8.6. (Serre's normality criterion).

(7.3)     Let Y be Noetherian of dimension one and generically reduced. For Y to be reduced, it is necessary and sufficient that Y be Cohen–Macaulay.

        EGA IV. 5.8.5.

(7.4)     Let f : X → Y be a morphism of flat S-schemes of finite presentation. For f to satisfy one of the following conditions: to be flat, smooth, étale, an open immersion

II    Generalized elliptic curves.

        In this chapter, we define generalized elliptic curves over an arbitrary base scheme and prove the theorems that make the adopted definition workable.

1. Néron polygons.

1.1.     Let C̃ = ℙ¹ × ℤ/n be the disjoint union of n copies of ℙ¹, indexed by ℤ/n (n ≥ 1). By gluing the i-th copy of ℙ¹ to the (i+1)-st, identifying the section 0 of the i-th copy with the section ∞ of the (i+1)-st, one obtains a genus-one curve C over Spec(ℤ), with normalization C̃.

        For every scheme S, the scheme over S obtained from this one by extension of scalars is called the standard Néron polygon with n sides over S, or simply the standard n-gon over S. A Néron polygon (respectively, an n-gon) over an algebraically closed field k is a scheme over k isomorphic to one of the standard polygons (respectively, to the standard n-gon).

Examples.

        n = 1

        n = 3

Lemma 1 2.     Let C be a Néron polygon over an algebraically closed field k.

(i)        H⁰(C,𝒪_C) = k.

(ii)       H⁰(C,ω_C) has dimension 1 over k, and the canonical morphism

        H⁰(C,ω_C) ⊗_k 𝒪_C → ω_C

is an isomorphism. In particular, ω_C ≃ 𝒪_C.

III. Representability theorems.

0. Introduction and notation.

In this chapter and those that follow, we define and study various algebraic stacks classifying generalized elliptic curves equipped with various additional structures.

0.1. Write 𝔐 for the category fibered in groupoids over the category (Sch) of schemes defined as follows: 𝔐(S) is the category whose objects are generalized elliptic curves over S and whose morphisms are S-isomorphisms; the functor "inverse image by u : S → T" is

        E ↦ E ×_T S.

The category 𝔐 is a stack over (Sch) for the fpqc topology (2.1), but it is not an algebraic stack.

0.2. Let 𝔐_* be the following substack of 𝔐: 𝔐_* classifies generalized elliptic curves C/S such that, for every geometric point s̄ of S, the characteristic of k(s̄) does not divide the number of irreducible components of the geometric fiber C_{s̄}. The principal result 2.5 of this chapter is that 𝔐_* is an algebraic stack. The representability theorems of the following chapters will follow from this technical theorem. We shall deduce it from M. Artin's general criteria. To apply them, the essential point will be to prove the effective prorepresentability of certain functors; this will be done in Section 1.

0.3. We adopt the following notational conventions.

a) 𝔐 with a subscript denotes the algebraic stack classifying generalized elliptic curves subject to certain restrictions or equipped with additional structures of the type indicated by the subscript.

b) The superscript o denotes the open substack corresponding to elliptic curves in the strict sense.

c) The superscript h denotes the open substack obtained by removing the points corresponding to supersingular elliptic curves in characteristic p dividing n, where n depends on the context.

d) The superscript ∞ denotes the closed substack that is the image of the singular locus of the curve

1. A prorepresentability theorem.

1.1 Let Λ be a complete local ring with residue field k and let C_o be a generalized elliptic curve over k. Assume that C_o is smooth or is the base change to k of the standard generalized elliptic curve with n sides (II.1.9). Let D be the deformation functor of C_o: for a complete local Noetherian Λ-algebra A with residue field k, D(A) is the set of isomorphism classes of generalized elliptic curves C/Spec(A), equipped with an isomorphism C ⊗_A k ≃ C_o. This section is devoted to the proof of the following theorem.

Theorem 1.2. Suppose that C_o is smooth or that n is prime to the characteristic exponent p of k. Then:

(i) (C_o,+) has no nonzero infinitesimal automorphisms.

(ii) The deformation functor D of (C_o,+) is effectively prorepresentable.

(iii) D is prorepresented by a curve C over Spec(Λ[[t]]).

(iv) If C_o is not smooth, t may be chosen so that t = 0 is the image of the non-smoothness subscheme.

The infinitesimal automorphisms of (C_o,+) form the group Lie Aut(C_o,+), so (i) follows from (II.1.10). It follows from (i) and [25] that D is prorepresentable.

1.3. The case in which C_o is irreducible.

In this case the deformation functor of (C_o,+) is identified by II.2.7 with the functor D' of deformations of (C_o,e), the pair consisting of the curve C_o and the marked section e. This latter functor is effectively prorepresentable, since a formal scheme in complete curves is always projective and hence algebraizable. That D' satisfies (iii) follows from the two formulas

(1.3.1)        dim Ext¹(Ω¹_{C_o}(e), 𝒪_{C_o}) = 1

(1.3.2)        dim Ext²(Ω¹_{C_o}(e), 𝒪_{C_o}) = 0.

Indeed, Ext² is the group in which the obstructions to deformations live. If it vanishes, D' is prorepresented by a formal power-series algebra over Λ. Ext¹ is identified with D'(k[ε]/(ε²)) and determines the relative dimension.

Let us prove (1.3.1) and (1.3.2). Since ω_{C_o} is isomorphic to 𝒪_{C_o}, duality (I.2.2) gives

Formula (1.3.2) follows trivially. For (1.3.1), we may suppose that k is algebraically closed.

2. Construction of 𝔪_*.

Lemma 2.1. The stack 𝔪 (defined in 0.1) is a stack for the fpqc topology.

Proof. Let S' → S be an fpqc morphism and let p' : C' → S' be a generalized elliptic curve equipped with descent data. The subschemes S'_n of S' defined in II.1.15 descend to subschemes S_n of S (fpqc descent of closed subschemes). By localizing on S for the Zariski topology, we may therefore suppose that the geometric fibers of C' are smooth or have n irreducible components. The subscheme C'_n of C' is then finite over S' (cf. II.1.20) and meets every irreducible component of every geometric fiber of C'. The invertible sheaf ℒ = 𝒪_{C'}(C'_n) is relatively ample and is equipped with descent data. The assertion thus follows from descent for quasi-projective schemes (SGA 1, VIII.7.8 and SGA 1, VIII.5.2).

Recall that for a stack 𝒢 over (Sch/S), the 1-morphisms ξ : X → 𝒢 from an S-scheme X to 𝒢 are identified with the objects of 𝒢(X) ([8]).

2.2. M. Artin proved a manageable criterion for showing that a functor is representable by an algebraic space ([2], [3]). The same proof gives the following criterion for verifying that a stack is algebraic.

Theorem 2.3 (M. Artin). Let S be a scheme of finite type over a field or over an excellent Dedekind ring. Let 𝒢 be a category fibered in groupoids over (Sch/S).

𝒢 is an algebraic stack locally of finite type over S if (and only if):

(0) 𝒢 is a stack for the étale topology.

(1) 𝒢 is locally of finite presentation; that is, for every filtered projective system of affine S-schemes Spec(A_i), the canonical functor

        lim→_i 𝒢(Spec(A_i)) → 𝒢(lim←_i Spec(A_i))

defines an equivalence of categories.

(2) Let ξ,η ∈ Ob(𝒢(X)) be two 1-morphisms from an S-scheme X of finite type over S to 𝒢. Then Isom(X; ξ,η) is an algebraic space locally of finite type over S.

(3) Let k_o be an 𝒪_S-field of finite type (that is, Spec(k_o) is of finite type over S), and let ξ_o be a 1-morphism from Spec(k_o) to 𝒢. There exist a complete local ring R, a morphism u from the spectrum of a finite separable extension k'_o of k_o into the closed point s of Spec(R), and a commutative diagram

        Spec(k'_o)  →  Spec(k_o)
            |              |
          u |              | ξ_o
            ↓              ↓
          Spec(R)   ──ξ──→ 𝒢

with ξ formally étale at s.

(4) If ξ is a 1-morphism from an S-scheme X of finite type into 𝒢 and ξ is formally étale at a point x of finite type over S, then ξ is formally étale at every point of finite type over S in an open neighborhood of x.

Remarks 2.4.

(i) If the residue fields of finite type of S are perfect, then, to establish that 𝒢 is an algebraic stack, one may replace (0)-(4) by (0), (1), (2), (3'), and (4), where (3') is the following condition.

(3') Let s ∈ S and let k_o be a finite extension of k(s). Suppose that u : Spec(k_o) → S is of finite type. By hypothesis k(s) is then perfect and k_o/k(s) is separable. There is therefore a unique complete local ring Λ(k_o) with residue field k_o, equipped with a formally étale morphism ū : Spec(Λ(k_o)) → S extending u.

For ξ_o ∈ Ob 𝒢(k_o), write Def(ξ_o) for the following category over the dual of Ĉ_{Λ(k_o)}: for A ∈ Ob Ĉ_{Λ(k_o)}, an object of Def(ξ_o)(A) is an object ξ of 𝒢(A), equipped with an isomorphism ξ_o →̃ (the image of ξ in 𝒢(k_o)). Condition (3') is the conjunction of (3'a) and (3'b):

(3'a) The objects of 𝒢 have no infinitesimal automorphisms; more precisely, for k_o and ξ_o as above, and for ξ'_o the pullback of ξ_o to k_o[ε] (ε² = 0), one has Aut(ξ'_o) →̃ Aut(ξ_o). This condition, together with (2), implies that the objects of Def(ξ_o)(A) have no nontrivial automorphisms.

(3'b) For k_o and ξ_o as above, the functor

        A → the set of isomorphism classes in Def(ξ_o)(A)

is effectively prorepresentable (by a complete local ring R and ξ ∈ 𝒢(R) reducing to ξ_o).

It even suffices to verify (3'b) after extension of scalars to a finite extension of k_o.

(ii) If S is of finite type over a field or over an excellent Dedekind ring having infinitely many points, and if the complete local rings R that occur in condition (3'b) are all normal and of the same Krull dimension, condition (4) may be omitted.

(For a reader familiar with [2], (i) is easy to prove. For (ii), see [2], Thm. 3.9).

Theorem 2.5.

(i) 𝔪_* (defined in 0.2) is an algebraic stack smooth over Spec(ℤ).

(ii) The image 𝔪_*^∞ of the non-smoothness scheme of the universal generalized elliptic curve over 𝔪_* is the union of the images of f_n (n ≥ 1).

Proof. To prove that 𝔪_* is an algebraic stack, we use criterion 2.3 (with S = Spec(ℤ)). Let us review conditions (0) through (4).

(0) follows from 2.1.

(1) follows from standard arguments in EGA IV.8.8.

(2) Let X be an S-scheme of finite type and let (p₁ : C₁ → X,+), (p₂ : C₂ → X,+) be two generalized elliptic curves. Let us prove that Isom_X((C₁,+),(C₂,+)) is representable. This functor is an fpqc sheaf (2.1), so the problem is local. We may therefore suppose that the geometric fibers of C₁ are smooth or n-sided, for a suitable n, and that there is a φ : ℤ/n ↪ C₁ whose image meets every irreducible component of every geometric fiber of C₁. The morphism f ↦ f∘φ(1) maps Isom into the open subscheme of C_n^reg consisting of those g for which the g^k meet all components of the geometric fibers. The following assertion implies that this morphism is relatively representable and hence that Isom is representable.

(*) For C_i with smooth or n-sided fibers, equipped with H_i ⊂ C_i^reg, with H_i isomorphic to ℤ/n and meeting all components of all geometric fibers (i=1,2), Isom((C₁,H₁,+),(C₂,H₂,+)) is representable.

By II 1.17, the morphism

        Isom((C₁,H₁,+),(C₂,H₂,+)) → Isom((C₁/H₁,e),(C₂/H₂,e))

is representable by an étale morphism, while the theory of the Hilbert functor implies that Isom((C₁/H₁,e),(C₂/H₂,e)) is representable.

In this chapter we define and study the moduli schemes of elliptic curves whose n-division points are equipped with additional structures. We study in detail the structure at infinity of these schemes. Their reduction modulo p, for p∣n, will not be considered seriously until the following chapter.

(iv) The pair (C,α) is unique up to a unique isomorphism.

Proof. (i) This is a theorem of Néron and Kodaira ([4] or [20] or [14]).

(ii) The universal property of the Néron model ensures that e ∈ C_η(η) extends to a section of C̃^reg over S. If u ∈ C̃^reg(S), the translation u+ on C_η extends by transport of structure to an automorphism of C̃; similarly, x → −x extends to C̃.

Let U be the largest open subset of C̃ such that the group law + of C_η extends to + : U × C → C. It is enough to prove that U = C̃^reg. Once this is established, the identities expressing that + is a generalized elliptic-curve structure follow from the schematic density of C_η in C̃. For v ∈ C̃^reg(S), U is stable under translation by v: extend + to v+U by (v+u) + x = v+(u+x). Since U is also stable under étale localization on S, as follows by descent and the compatibility of minimal-model formation with étale localization on S, it is enough to show that U_s ≠ ∅.

Let x be a maximal, hence generic, point of C̃_s, and let S₁ be the trait given by the spectrum of the local ring of C̃ at x. Since C̃ is smooth over S at x, C̃₁ = C̃ ×_S S₁ is again a minimal model over S₁. Let u ∈ C₁(S) be defined by the inclusion S₁ ↪ C̃. By transport of structure, translation by u on the generic fiber of C̃₁ extends to an automorphism of C₁, whence

        + : S₁ ×_S C̃ → C̃.

Writing S₁ as the projective limit of the neighborhoods of x, one finds that the morphism + : C_η × C_η → C_η extends to + : U ×_S C̃ → C̃, with x ∈ U.

(iii) We know that C̃_n is quasi-finite and flat. By the hypothesis and the universal property of the Néron model, all geometric points of (C_η̄)_n come from sections of C̃_n over S. This group is therefore finite over S, and (C̃_s)_n has rank n². Thus the special fiber C̃_s is smooth or an m-gon, with n∣m (cf. II 1.13), and 1.3 is applied to obtain C by contraction.

(iv) Let C be a generalized elliptic curve over S, with generic fiber C_η, and suppose that C_s is smooth or an n-gon. At a non-smooth point u of C, the formal completion of C is isomorphic to the completion at the origin of the affine curve in A_S² with equation xy = t^k, for a suitable k. By homogeneity, k does not depend on the point chosen. For k > 1, C is singular at u. These singularities are resolved by repeatedly blowing up the singular points, a process that replaces u by k−1 projective lines:

             u

(cf. [8]). Let C̃ be the resolved curve. There is no exceptional curve of the first kind contained in C̃_s, so C̃ is the minimal model of C_η. The curve C is smooth if and only if the minimal model C̃ of C_η is smooth, in which case C = C̃. Otherwise C̃_s is a Néron nk-gon, and C is obtained from it by contraction in the manner used in the existence proof.

2. Level-n structures.

2.1. Let n be an integer. In this section we consider only schemes S on which n is invertible.

In this section, 𝔪_(n) denotes the algebraic stack over ℤ[1/n] classifying generalized elliptic curves C/S whose geometric fibers are smooth or Néron n-gons. By (II.1.15), 𝔪_(n) is an open substack of 𝔪_* and hence an algebraic stack, smooth over ℤ[1/n] by (III.2.5). Let f_n be the section of 𝔪_(n) defined by curve 1.9 over ℤ[1/n].

Proposition 2.2. The algebraic stack 𝔪_(n) is proper and smooth over ℤ[1/n]. Its locus at infinity 𝔪_(n)^∞ = 𝔪_(n) ∩ 𝔪_*^∞ is the image of f_n.

The second assertion is included only as a reminder. It follows from III.2.5 and implies that 𝔪_(n)^o is dense in 𝔪_(n). Properness then follows from 1.6 and the valuative criterion for properness [8].

        α : C_n →̃ (ℤ/n)².

Definition 2.4. 𝔪_n[1/n] is the following algebraic stack over ℤ[1/n]: for a scheme S on which n is invertible, 𝔪_n[1/n](S) is the category of generalized elliptic curves C/S whose geometric fibers are smooth or Néron n-gons, equipped with a level-n structure.

It is clear that 𝔪_n[1/n] is finite étale and representable over 𝔪_(n), and is in fact a principal homogeneous space under GL(2,ℤ/n). We write 𝔪_n^∞[1/n] for the inverse image of 𝔪_(n)^∞, the image of the non-smoothness subscheme of the universal curve over 𝔪_n[1/n]. The following theorem follows immediately from 2.2.

Theorem 2.5. 𝔪_n[1/n] is proper and smooth over ℤ[1/n], and 𝔪_n^∞[1/n] is finite étale over ℤ[1/n].

2.6. Recall that an algebraic stack 𝒢 “is” an algebraic space when the objects it classifies have no automorphisms. More precisely, if for every algebraically closed field k the objects of 𝒢(k) have no nontrivial automorphisms, then

(a) for every scheme S, the objects of 𝒢(S) have no nontrivial automorphisms;

(b) the functor S ↦ (the set of isomorphism classes in 𝒢(S)) is representable by an algebraic space.

Theorem 2.7. If n ≥ 3, 𝔪_n[1/n] is an algebraic space.

Let C be a generalized elliptic curve over an algebraically closed field k, either smooth or a Néron n-gon. One must prove that an automorphism σ of C that is trivial on C_n is the identity. When C is an elliptic curve, apply ([26], appendix to Exposé 17). When C is a Néron polygon, II.1.10 shows that Aut(C) acts faithfully on C_n.

Variant 2.8. This argument, together with III.2.1, also immediately implies that the functor

        F_n : S ↦ (the set of isomorphism classes of generalized elliptic curves over S equipped with a level-n structure)

is a sheaf for the fpqc topology. The arguments of III.2.5 then show that this functor satisfies M. Artin's representability criterion. To prove that F_n is representable by an algebraic space for n ≥ 3, it is therefore unnecessary first to generalize M. Artin's criterion to algebraic stacks.

Corollary 2.9. If n ≥ 3, 𝔪_n[1/n] is a projective smooth scheme over ℤ[1/n].

Indeed, a regular algebraic space in curves over ℤ is always quasi-projective, and hence a scheme. Here is a more constructive proof: by transcendental methods (cf. §5), one verifies that after extension of scalars to ℂ, 𝔪_n^∞ meets every irreducible component of 𝔪_n. By specialization it follows that the divisor 𝔪_n^∞ meets every irreducible component of every geometric fiber of 𝔪_n; here one uses that 𝔪_n is proper and smooth. Consequently 𝒪(𝔪_n^∞) is a relatively ample invertible sheaf.

3. Level-H structures.

3.1. Let n be an integer and H a subgroup of GL(2,ℤ/n). Let S be a scheme on which n is invertible and C an elliptic curve over S. For every S-scheme T, let F(T) be the set of level-n structures on C_T, the inverse image of C over T. The functor F is represented by a finite étale cover of S that is a principal homogeneous space under GL(2,ℤ/n). Let F_H be the sheaf for the étale topology generated by the presheaf

        T ↦ F_H(T) = F(T)/H.

(Since H acts on the left, it might be better to write H\F(T).) In canonical language,

        F_H = Hom(C_n,(ℤ/n)²)/H.

This functor is represented by a finite étale cover of S.

A level-H structure on C is an element of F_H(S). An isomorphism α : C_n →̃ (ℤ/n)² defines a level-H structure, and two such isomorphisms define the same structure if and only if, locally on S, there is a g ∈ H such that gα = β. This g is uniquely determined and hence constant on each connected component of S. One should keep in mind that a level-H structure does not in general arise from an α : C_n →̃ (ℤ/n)². It arises from such an α only locally for the étale topology. For example, when H = GL(2,ℤ/n), C has exactly one level-H structure; it comes from an α only if C_n is isomorphic to (ℤ/n)² over S.

Definition 3.2. 𝔪_H^o[1/n] is the following algebraic stack: for a scheme S on which n is invertible, 𝔪_H^o[1/n](S) is the category of elliptic curves C/S equipped with a level-H structure, with isomorphisms as morphisms.

It is clear that 𝔪_H^o[1/n] is finite étale and locally representable over 𝔪_1^o[1/n].

Definition 3.3. The algebraic stack 𝔪_H is the normalization of 𝔪_1 in 𝔪_H^o[1/n].

Theorem 3.4. (i) 𝔪_H is proper over Spec(ℤ).

(ii) 𝔪_H[1/n] is smooth over Spec(ℤ[1/n]), and 𝔪_H^o[1/n] is the complement of a substack 𝔪_H^∞[1/n] that is finite étale over Spec(ℤ[1/n]).

Proof. (i) By definition, 𝔪_H is finite and relatively representable over 𝔪_1. Its properness therefore follows from that of 𝔪_1.

(ii) The assertion follows from Abhyankar's lemma (SGA 1, XIII 5), which applies here because 𝔪_1[1/n] is smooth over ℤ[1/n], because 𝔪_1^∞[1/n] is a divisor of 𝔪_1[1/n], smooth over ℤ[1/n] and with generic point of characteristic zero, and because 𝔪_H^o[1/n] is finite étale over 𝔪_1[1/n] − 𝔪_1^∞[1/n].

In 6.7 we shall give a “modular” proof of 3.4.

Construction 1.4 defines a morphism of stacks

Proposition 3.9. With the notation of 3.7, the isomorphism of 3.8 extends to

(3.9.1)        𝔪_K ×_{𝔪_1} 𝔪_L →̃ 𝔪_{K∩L}.

Proof. It is enough to prove that 𝔪_K ×_{𝔪_1} 𝔪_L is normal. We prove this over ℤ[1/m]; over ℤ[1/n] the argument is symmetric. The stack 𝔪_L[1/m] is smooth over ℤ and hence flat over 𝔪_1 by (I.7.1). Thus 𝔪_K ×_{𝔪_1} 𝔪_L[1/m] is flat over 𝔪_K and Cohen-Macaulay by (I.7.2 and I.7.1). Moreover 𝔪_L^o[1/m] is étale over 𝔪_1, so 𝔪_K ×_{𝔪_1} 𝔪_L^o[1/m], being étale over 𝔪_K, is normal.

By Abhyankar's lemma, the ramification of 𝔪_K[1/n] over 𝔪_1[1/n] (respectively of 𝔪_L[1/m] over 𝔪_1[1/m]) is tame. The ramification indices for 𝔪_K and 𝔪_L are therefore relatively prime; in fact they divide n and m. Hence 𝔪_K[1/mn] ×_{𝔪_1} 𝔪_L[1/mn] is smooth, and Serre's criterion (I.7.2) completes the proof.

Corollary 3.9.2. If n is the product of two relatively prime integers and n ≥ 3, then 𝔪_n is a scheme.

Write n=n'n''. The stack 𝔪_n[1/n'] is a scheme because it is representable over 𝔪_{n'}[1/n]. Likewise 𝔪_n[1/n''] is a scheme; therefore 𝔪_n is a scheme.

(iii) One has M_H=M_n/H.

(iv) The geometric fibers of M_H[1/n] → Spec(ℤ[1/n]) are geometrically unibranch.

Lemma 3.17. Let E be an elliptic curve over an algebraically closed field k and let b be an integer. There are only finitely many subgroup schemes of E of rank b.

Proof of 3.17. Proceed by induction on b.

(a) There are only finitely many étale subgroup schemes of E of rank b: they identify with the subgroups of order b in E_b(k).

(b) If H⊂E is not étale, then k has characteristic p>0 and H contains Ker(F). Thus the non-étale subgroup schemes of E of rank b correspond to the subgroup schemes of rank b/p of E^(p)=E/Ker(F), and the induction hypothesis applies.

Proof of 3.16, continued. Construction 3.14 defines a section s over 𝔪_K^o⊗Spec(ℚ) of I×_{𝔪_1^o}𝔪_K^o.

By Zariski's Main Theorem and the normality of 𝔪_K^o, this section extends over 𝔪_K^o, defining a subgroup B of the pullback E, along c, of the universal elliptic curve over 𝔪_1^o. The required extension cg is defined by E/B, and the isomorphism [g] is defined as in 3.15.

The resulting morphism cg is quasi-finite and representable. It therefore identifies 𝔪_K^o with an open substack of the normalization 𝔪_{gKg⁻¹}^o of 𝔪_1^o in

        𝔪_K^o⊗Spec(ℚ) ──g→̃ 𝔪_{gKg⁻¹}^o⊗Spec(ℚ),

and hence gives

        g:𝔪_K^o↪𝔪_{gKg⁻¹}^o.

This morphism is an isomorphism, with inverse g⁻¹.

3.18. One can show that g extends to an isomorphism

        𝔪_K→̃𝔪_{gKg⁻¹}.

We shall only prove the analogous result for the coarse schemes.

Lemma 4.18. Let (C,α) be a generalized elliptic curve over an algebraically closed field, equipped with a projective level-n structure. If n≥2, the only nontrivial automorphism of C preserving α is x↦-x.

For an n-gon the lemma follows easily from II.1.10 and is true even for n=1. For smooth C it is a special case of the following lemma.

Lemma 4.19. Let n≥2 and let g be a finite-order automorphism of an abelian variety X over an algebraically closed field k. If g acts as a scalar on X_n, then g²=1.

By hypothesis there is r∈ℤ/n such that g-r vanishes on X_n. Hence g-r=n·h for some endomorphism h of X. If ζ is a root of the characteristic polynomial of g, then ζ is a root of unity and the algebraic integer ζ-r is divisible by n. Let R be the ring of integers of ℚ(ζ). The image of ζ in R/nR is therefore the image of r. Since R=ℤ[ζ], this is impossible unless ζ=±1. Since g is semisimple, the assertion follows.

6. Level-H structures: study at infinity.

This section will not be used later in the article. We recommend omitting it on a first reading.

Let H be a subgroup of GL(2,ℤ/n). We seek a modular interpretation of 𝔪_H[1/n] generalizing 3.5, 4.13, 4.14, 4.15, and 4.20. We shall first define modularly a stack ′𝔪_H[1/n], proper and smooth over ℤ[1/n], with 𝔪_H^o[1/n] as a dense open substack. As in 3.5 we define a finite morphism c:′𝔪_H[1/n]→𝔪_1[1/n]. We then prove the analogue of (3.5.1); the proof of 3.5 gives ′𝔪_H[1/n]=𝔪_H[1/n], the desired modular interpretation.

6.1. Let A be a group isomorphic to (ℤ/n)^2, let A'⊂A be a subgroup isomorphic to ℤ/n, and let B contain A'. For a suitable divisor m of n, (A,A',B) is isomorphic to

        ((ℤ/n)^2,ℤ/n×{0},ℤ/n×mℤ/nℤ).

Let μ also be isomorphic to ℤ/n, let β_0:Λ²A→̃μ, and denote by β_1 its restriction to Λ²B.

The essential example is a generalized elliptic curve C over a complete trait S with points η and s. Let η̄ be the spectrum of an algebraic closure of k(η), and s̄ the spectrum of the corresponding algebraic closure of k(s). If n is invertible on S, C_{η̄} is smooth, and C_{s̄} is an m-sided Néron polygon with m|n, take

        μ=μ_n(η̄)≃μ_n(s̄), A=C_n(η̄), A'=C_n^o(s̄),
        B=(C_s^{reg})_n(s̄), and β_0=e_n.

The restriction β_1 of β_0 to Λ²B depends only on the special fiber C_{s̄}; see 3.21.

6.2. Let I be the set of isomorphisms α:A→(ℤ/n)^2, and let Ī be the set of pairs (ᾱ,β), with ᾱ:B↪(ℤ/n)^2 and β:μ→̃ℤ/n, for which

                         Λ²ᾱ
              Λ²B  ─────────────→  Λ²(ℤ/n)^2
               │ β_1                    │ s
               ↓                        ↓
               μ  ────────β────────→   ℤ/n

commutes. This is diagram (6.2.1).

V. Reduction modulo p.

In this chapter we study the reduction modulo p of the stacks 𝔪_K, for K = Γ_0(p), Γ_∞(p), and Γ(p^k). Comparison of the results obtained for Γ_0(p) and Γ_∞(p) allows us to show that, in accordance with a conjecture of Shimura, certain abelian schemes studied by Shimura and Casselman [5] have good reduction over the ring of integers of suitable cyclotomic extensions of ℚ.

1. Study of 𝔪_{Γ_0(p)}.

In this section we propose to give a modular interpretation of the stack 𝔪_{Γ_0(p)} when p is prime. Some preliminary results will be used again in the following sections.

1.1. Let 𝒢_n be the stack classifying generalized elliptic curves C/S with geometrically irreducible fibers, equipped with a subgroup scheme A locally isomorphic to μ_n (for the étale topology), that is, finite flat locally free of rank n with étale Cartier dual.

Proposition 1.2. The morphism "forget A" : 𝒢_n → 𝔪_1 is étale; in particular, 𝒢_n is an algebraic stack smooth over ℤ.

Let C/S be classified by 𝔪_1. It must be checked that the functor

        F : (Sch/S) → (Sets),

which assigns to T/S the set of subgroups A of (C_T)_n locally isomorphic to μ_n, is represented by a scheme M étale over S. Representability follows from the theory of the Hilbert scheme; M is étale because it is formally étale (SGA 3 IX 3.6).

1.3. Let ℬ_n be the stack classifying generalized elliptic curves C/S whose geometric fibers are smooth or n-gons, equipped with a subgroup scheme B locally isomorphic to ℤ/n (for the étale topology) that meets every irreducible component of every geometric fiber.

Let (C,B) be as above. The group scheme B acts freely on C

Lemma 1.13. Let f : X → S be a finite morphism of Noetherian schemes, with S reduced. If the rank of the geometric fibers of f is constant, then f is flat.

One may suppose that S is the spectrum of a local ring A and that X is the spectrum of a finite A-algebra B. If ∑ λ_i e_i = 0, with λ_i ∈ A, the hypothesis implies that the λ_i vanish modulo every prime ideal, and hence vanish because A is reduced; thus the A-module B is free with basis the e_i.

Theorem 1.16. (i) The maps Φ_1 and Φ_2 = wΦ_1 are closed immersions. Their images are the two irreducible components of 𝔪_{Γ_0(p)}ᵒ ⊗ 𝔽_p.

(ii) These irreducible components meet transversely at the supersingular points. The stack 𝔪_{Γ_0(p)} ⊗ 𝔽_p, which is reduced, therefore has no singularities other than ordinary double points.

(iii) 𝔪_{Γ_0(p)} is regular.

Use a superscript h to denote the stack obtained by removing the supersingular points of characteristic p. One checks that Φ_1 and wΦ_1 define an isomorphism

        Φ_1 ⨿ wΦ_1 : 𝔪_1^{oh} ⊗ 𝔽_p ⨿ 𝔪_1^{oh} ⊗ 𝔽_p →̃ 𝔪_{Γ_0(p)}^{oh} ⊗ 𝔽_p.

The inverse isomorphism is defined by c and cw, restricted to the images of Φ_1 and wΦ_1.

That Φ_1 (respectively wΦ_1) is a closed immersion follows from the existence of a retraction (since these are representable morphisms). It is known (IV.5.6) that 𝔪_1 ⊗ 𝔽_p is geometrically irreducible, and this proves (i).

The stack 𝔪_{Γ_0(p)} is reduced because it is Cohen--Macaulay and generically reduced (I.7.3). Since at a supersingular point 𝔪_{Γ_0(p)} → Spec(ℤ) has an ordinary quadratic singularity, (I.5.2) shows that there exists k ∈ ℕ such that the completion of the strict local ring of 𝔪_{Γ_0(p)} at such a point is isomorphic to

        W(𝔽̄_p)[[X,Y]]/(X.Y - p^k)    (W = Witt vectors).

This is absurd, because by [22] α_p admits no lifting over W(𝔽̄_p)/(p^k) when k > 1.

The stack ′𝔪_{Γ′_∞(p)} ⊗ Λ_p is finite and representable over 𝔪_{Γ_0(p)} ⊗ Λ_p. It therefore suffices to prove that ′𝔪_{Γ′_∞(p)} ⊗ Λ_p is normal at the supersingular points. The following lemma shows that ′𝔪_{Γ′_∞(p)} ⊗ Λ_p is in fact regular at these points.

Lemma 2.8. Let s̄ be a supersingular geometric point of characteristic p of 𝔪_{Γ_0(p)}. Let Ŝ be the completion of the strict henselization of 𝔪_{Γ_0(p)} at s̄, equipped with its unique Λ_p-algebra structure. Let (C,A) over Ŝ be defined by Ŝ → 𝔪_{Γ_0(p)}, and let (L,a,b) be defined by A.

(i)        Ŝ ≃ W(𝔽̄_p)[[u,v]]/(uv-w(χ))    with (L,a,b) ≃ (𝒪,u,v).

(ii) The normalization ′𝔪_{Γ′_∞(p)} ⊗_{𝔪_{Γ_0(p)}} Ŝ of Ŝ in Isom_{Ŝ[ζ_p,1/p]}(ℤ/p,A) is Ŝ-isomorphic to

        W(𝔽̄_p)[[ζ_p,x,y]]/(xy-w(χ,ζ)) ≃ W(𝔽̄_p)[[x,y]]/(x^{p-1} y^{p-1} - w(χ)),

with x^{p-1} = u and y^{p-1} = v.

It is known that Ŝ ≃ W(𝔽̄_p)[[u,v]]/(uv - p) (1.16), that ab = w(χ) = p times a unit (cf. 2.5), and that a and b vanish at the supersingular points (2.4.4). Assertions (i) and (ii) follow.

Remark 2.9. It follows from 2.4, 2.4.4, and 2.8(ii) that Ŝ, equipped with A, is a versal formal moduli scheme for deformations of α_p.

a) a morphism ℤ/p →̃ H over S[1/p];

b) over S ⊗ Λ_p, where H defines (L,a,b), sections x of L* and y of L such that x^{p-1} = a, y^{p-1} = b, and xy = w(χ,ζ).

Let v be a characteristic-p point of ℤ[ζ_n,ζ_p]^H, and let \overline{k(v)} be an algebraic closure of its residue field. Let ν be the number of supersingular points of M_{Γ(n)} ⊗_{ℤ[ζ]} \overline{k(v)}. The scheme M_{Γ(n)} ⊗_{ℤ[ζ]} \overline{k(v)} is known to be irreducible. is an extension of an abelian scheme by a torus of dimension ν - 1 (cf. I. 3.7). In particular:

Proposition 3.3. The abelian variety J(n,H) over ℚ[ζ_n,ζ_p]^H has semistable reduction at the places dividing p.

Suppose 0 → A → B → C → 0 is an exact sequence up to isogeny of abelian varieties over the fraction field of a discrete valuation ring. Let α_ab, α_m, and α_add denote the abelian, multiplicative, and unipotent ranks of the special fiber of the Néron model. Then

        α_ab(A) - α_ab(B) + α_ab(C) = 0,

and likewise for α_m and α_add. Moreover, if α_add = 0, then α_ab and α_m are invariant under scalar extension (the semistable case). The condition α_add = α_m = 0 is equivalent to good reduction. Here α_add(J(n,H)) = 0 and α_m(J(n,H)) = ν-1, independently of H; the theorem follows.

4.20. By 4.17 and 4.19, the irreducible components of 𝔪_n ⊗_{ℤ[ζ_n]} 𝔽̄_p are indexed by P = ℙ^1(ℤ/p^k), meet only at the supersingular points, and are unibranch. The following theorem asserts that all the irreducible components meet at every supersingular point.

Theorem 4.20. The morphism 𝔪_n → 𝔪_m is totally ramified at the supersingular points of characteristic p.

Let E₀ be a supersingular elliptic curve over F̄_p, and let E/Ŝ be the formal moduli scheme of E₀ over W(F̄_p). We have Ŝ ≃ W(F̄_p)[[t]]; it is the completion of the strict henselization of 𝔪₁ at the given geometric point.

Lemma 4.21. The partition 𝒫 is independent of E₀.

Proof. Let E₀ and E′₀ be two supersingular elliptic curves over F̄_p, let Ŝ and Ŝ′ be their formal moduli schemes over W(F̄_p), let E and E′ be their universal deformations over Ŝ and Ŝ′, and let T̂ and T̂′ be as in 4.20.

                        E ──φ──→ E′

in which φ extends φ₀. The isogeny φ induces an isomorphism from E_{p^k} to E′_{p^k}, hence an isomorphism φ_T : T̂ → T̂′ above φ_S.

VI. Coarse moduli schemes.

In this chapter we study coarse moduli schemes, in particular the relation between 𝔪_H and M_H. Some classical results are proved by "pure thought". The result of § 5 is made more precise in the following chapter.

1. The modular invariant.

Theorem 1.1. The coarse space M_1 and 𝔪_1 is isomorphic to ℙ^1_ℤ.

Characteristics 2 and 3 make the direct verification of 1.1 somewhat laborious. We shall deduce 1.1 from its corollary

(1.1.1)        M_{1ℂ} ≃ ℙ^1_ℂ.

a) M_1 is proper and flat over Spec(ℤ), normal and hence Cohen--Macaulay (I.7.2), and the geometric fibers of M_1 over Spec(ℤ) are irreducible.

We already know that M_1 is proper, flat, normal, with geometrically unibranch fibers (IV. 3.10). By 1.1.1 (or IV 5.4), the geometric generic fiber of M_1 is connected. All geometric fibers of M_1 are therefore connected (Zariski) and, being unibranch, are irreducible.

b) The geometric fibers of M_1 over Spec(ℤ) are reduced.

Let G be the open substack of 𝔪_1 corresponding to generalized curves having no automorphisms other than Id and x ↦ -x. It is open because, for C/S a curve classified by 𝔪_1, Aut_S(C) is finite and unramified over S (a consequence of the fact that 𝔪_1 is separated).

The map G → M_1 is étale, so its image A is smooth over ℤ. One verifies that G ⊃ 𝔪_1^∞. The fibers of A are therefore nonempty; by a), they are dense in the fibers of M_1. The (M_1)_{s̄} are thus generically reduced; being Cohen--Macaulay, they are in fact reduced.

c) End of the proof.

By invariance of the arithmetic genus under specialization, and by (1.1.1), one finds that the geometric fibers of M_1 are integral and have arithmetic genus 0. They are therefore isomorphic to the projective line. In particular, M_1 is proper and smooth over ℤ.

The Néron polygon with one side over Spec(ℤ) defines a section of M_1, with image M_1^∞. Fiber by geometric fiber one verifies that H^1(M_1,𝒪(M_1^∞)) = 0, and then that H^0(M_1,𝒪(M_1^∞)) is locally free of rank 2 over ℤ and its formation is compatible with passage to geometric fibers. Since ℤ is principal, H^0(M_1,𝒪(M_1^∞)) is free and has a basis {1,j}. Fiber by geometric fiber one verifies that 𝒪(M_1^∞) is very ample and that j defines an isomorphism

        M_1 →̃ ℙ^1_ℤ.

Proof of (1.1.1) Here are two classical proofs of (1.1.1).

(1) One verifies that M_1^o(ℂ) is the quotient of the Poincaré half-plane by SL(2,ℤ) (IV 5.4). Drawing a fundamental domain, one finds that M_1^o(ℂ) is homeomorphic to ℝ^2. The space M_1(ℂ), obtained from it by adjoining one point, is therefore a sphere.

(2) Over ℂ, the moduli scheme classifying integral generalized elliptic curves equipped with an invariant differential is

        Spec(ℂ[g_2,g_3]) - (the point g_2 = g_3 = 0),

with universal curve, in nonhomogeneous coordinates,

        ⎧ Y^2 = 4X^3 - g_2 X - g_3
        ⎩ ω = dX/Y                                      ([33] 2.5)

M_1 is the quotient of this scheme by 𝔾_m acting by

        λ.(g_2,g_3) = (λ^4 g_2,λ^6 g_3),

and is easily identified with ℙ^1.

The irreducibility of the fibers of M_1 over ℤ has the following corollary.

Corollary 1.2. Let k be an algebraically closed field of characteristic p. There are only finitely many isomorphism classes of supersingular elliptic curves over k.

The set of points of (M_1)_k corresponding to generalized elliptic curves E for which the Frobenius kernel is of multiplicative type is open and contains the point at infinity. Its complement, which corresponds to supersingular curves, is therefore finite.

1.3. The function j introduced in 1.1 c) is not uniquely determined; the ambiguity is j ↦ ± j + n (n ∈ ℤ). A choice of j, recalled below, is classical.

Let C/S be a generalized elliptic curve with irreducible fibers over S. Tate's formulary [33] explains how to associate with C/S a section j of ℙ^1 over S, with j = ∞ wherever C is singular. By the universal property of M_1, this morphism j : 𝔪_1 → ℙ^1 factors through j : M_1 → ℙ^1. One readily checks that j : M_1(ℂ) → ℙ^1(ℂ) is bijective [33]. The morphism j is dominant, flat (I 7.1.), and of degree one, hence an isomorphism. In particular, over every algebraically closed field k, j(C_1) = j(C_2) if and only if C_1 is isomorphic to C_2. This is proved by brute force in [33].

The function j is called the modular invariant.

1.4. Let C be an irreducible generalized elliptic curve over an algebraically closed field k. It is proved in [33] that Aut(C) = {±1} if and only if j(C) ≠ 0,2^6.3^3. Over the open subset of 𝔪_1 where j ≠ 0, 2^6.3^3, Aut(C) (with C the universal curve) is therefore locally constant. Hence:

Lemma 1.5. 𝔪_1 → M_1 is étale away from the sections j = 0,2^6 3^3 of M_1.

By contrast, 𝔪_1 is ramified over M_1 along these sections. Because of this ramification, there can be no section M_1 → 𝔪_1, i.e. there is no

1.8. Let C be the universal elliptic curve over 𝔪_1^o, and let γ be the morphism

Aut(C) → Aut(Lie(C)) ≃ 𝔾_m. We extract from [33] the following result about Aut(C).

Lemma 1.9. Over the substack of 𝔪_1^o[1/6] defined by c_4 = 0 (resp. c_6 = 0) (i.e. ³√j = 0, resp. ²√(j-1728) = 0), γ is an isomorphism Aut(C) →̃ μ_6 (resp. Aut(C) →̃ μ_4).

2. Automorphisms of elliptic curves. Criterion for 𝔪_H^o = M_H^o.

2.1. For an algebraic stack to be an algebraic space, it is necessary and sufficient that its geometric points have no nontrivial automorphisms. Thus, if H ⊂ GL(2, ℤ/n), in order that 𝔪_H^o[1/n] = M_H^o[1/n] (resp. 𝔪_H[1/n] = M_H[1/n]), it is necessary and sufficient that an elliptic curve (resp. generalized elliptic curve) equipped with an H-level structure, over an algebraically closed field k of characteristic p ∤ n, have no nontrivial automorphism.

For example, 𝔪_n[1/n] = M_n[1/n] for n ≥ 3 (IV 2.7).

In [32], the automorphisms of elliptic curves are described explicitly, so the preceding criterion is effective. The calculations of [33] show that characteristics 2 and 3 are exceptional, while the others are "like" characteristic 0. We propose to verify this point a priori. So as not to seem too ridiculous, we shall also treat the case of abelian varieties.

Lemma 2.2. Let (A, θ) be a polarized abelian variety over an algebraically closed field k of characteristic p > 0, and let φ be an automorphism of (A, θ). It is known that φ has finite order. If the degree of θ and the order of φ are prime to p, the triple (A, θ, φ) lifts to the ring of Witt vectors W(k).

There is no obstruction to deforming (A, θ): the formal moduli scheme of (A, θ) over W(k) is a scheme

        M = Spec(W/k)[[t_1...t_r]]        (k = ½ dim(A) (dim(A) + 1)).

Continuing the proof of Lemma 2.2, interpret φ as the action on (A, θ) of a cyclic group G whose order is prime to p. By transport of structure, G acts on the formal moduli scheme M: the automorphism φ of (A, θ) extends to an automorphism of M and of the universal deformation (A_M, θ_M) of (A, θ) over M. The formal moduli scheme of (A, θ, φ) is the G-fixed subscheme M^G of M. Since the order of G is prime to p, this subscheme is smooth over W(k), hence admits sections over W(k), and this proves 2.2.

Proposition 2.3. Let A be an abelian variety of dimension g over an algebraically closed field. Let φ be an automorphism of prime order q, and write

        A^φ =_dfn Ker(φ - id_A).

There is an integer k such that

        2.g = dim(A^φ) + k.(q-1).

Proof: Passing from A to A/A^φ, we reduce to the case in which A^φ is finite.

The characteristic polynomial of φ acting on A has integer coefficients, does not have 1 as a root, and has only qth roots of unity as roots. It is therefore a power of the cyclotomic polynomial, which has degree q-1. Comparing degrees proves the lemma.

Corollary 2.4. Let A be an abelian variety of dimension g over an algebraically closed field. Let φ be an automorphism of A of finite order. Every prime factor of the order of φ is smaller than 2g + 1.

Proof: This follows from 2.4.

Corollary 2.5. Let (A, θ) be a polarized abelian variety of dimension g over an algebraically closed field k of characteristic p, with polarization degree prime to p. Suppose that p > 2g + 1. If φ is an automorphism of (A, θ), then (A, θ, φ) lifts to characteristic 0 (over W(k)).

Proof: This follows from 2.2 and 2.4.

2.6. An elliptic curve has a canonical principal polarization. By 2.6, if φ is an automorphism of an elliptic curve E over an algebraically closed field k of characteristic p > 3, (E,φ) lifts to characteristic 0 (over W(k)).

Theorem 2.7. For 𝔪_H^o[1/6n] to be an algebraic space, it is necessary and sufficient that the inverse image Γ of H in SL(2,ℤ) have no finite-order element other than 1.

Let (E,ᾱ) be an elliptic curve equipped with a level-H structure over an algebraically closed field k of characteristic p = 0 or p > 3, with p ∤ n. We must show that every automorphism φ of (E,ᾱ) is trivial. By 2.6, (E,φ), and hence (E,ᾱ,φ), lifts to characteristic 0, so it is enough to treat the case p = 0.

The structure ᾱ defines an inclusion (IV.3.20) ℚ[ζ_n]^{det H} ⊂ k. We may reduce to the case in which k has finite absolute transcendence degree; then there is an embedding k ↪ ℂ inducing the identity inclusion of ℚ[ζ_n] in ℂ. This reduces us to k = ℂ, with ᾱ represented by a determinant-one isomorphism α : E_n →̃ (ℤ/n)^2.

If β : ℤ^2 → H_1(E(ℂ),ℤ) lifts the inverse of α (via IV 5.2.1), one verifies that Aut(E,ᾱ) is the stabilizer of z(β) (IV 5.1) in Γ. If Aut(E,ᾱ) ≠ {e}, Γ therefore has elements of finite order.

Conversely, every finite-order element φ of Γ has a fixed point in X, corresponding to (E,ᾱ,φ) over ℂ.

3. Rational points of coarse schemes.

3.1. Let H ⊂ GL(2, ℤ/n). An elliptic curve E equipped with a level-H structure α over a field k defines a point of M_H^o(k). Conversely, if x ∈ M_H^o[1/n](k), all one knows is that over the separable closure k̄ of k there exists a pair (E,α) defining x. The isomorphism class of (E,α) is invariant under Gal(k̄/k).

If (E,α) comes from (E_0,α_0) over k, the set of k-isomorphism classes of curves (E_1,α_1) defining x is canonically H^1(Gal(k̄/k),A̲u̲t̲(E_0,α_0)(k̄)). The obstruction to the existence of an (E_0,α_0) lies in an H^2 (in Giraud's sense). In the special case where Aut(E,α) is commutative, Gal(k̄/k) acts on Aut(E,α), and the obstruction lies in H^2(Gal(k̄/k),Aut(E,α)).

Proposition 3.2. Let k be a field of characteristic p and let H ⊂ GL(2, ℤ/n). Assume that p ∤ n. Every point x ∈ M_H^o(k) is defined by an elliptic curve E over k equipped with a level-H structure.

Proof (after J.P. Serre and J.S. Milne). Choose a separable closure k̄ of k and an object (E,α) over k̄ that defines the image of x in M_H^o(k̄). If H = GL(2, ℤ/n), which amounts to assuming n = 1, Proposition 3.2 reduces to 1.7. In the language of 3.1, a certain obstruction ε(E) is therefore zero. If Aut(E,α) is trivial, Proposition 3.2 is clear. If Aut(E) is reduced to ± 1 and Aut(E,α) is nontrivial, then Aut(E,α) →̃ Aut(E); the obstructions ε(E,α) and ε(E) to defining (E,α) or E over k are therefore equal and zero. To complete the proof, it is enough to treat the following two cases.

Case 1: p ≠ 2,3. By 1.9, Aut(E) is then μ_2, μ_4, or μ_6. The automorphism group Aut(E,α) of (E,α) is a subgroup of Aut(E). Proposition 3.2 says that the obstruction class ε(E,α) ∈ H^2(Gal(k̄/k), Aut(E,α)) is zero. By 1.7 its image ε(E) in H^2(Gal(k̄/k), Aut(E)) is zero, and we apply the following lemma.

Lemma 3.3. Let n be prime to p.

(i) The subgroups of μ_n are the μ_m, for m|n.

(ii) The map H^2(Gal(k̄/k), μ_m) → Gal(k̄/k, μ_n) is injective.

Proof. We leave the proof of (i) to the reader. Consider the long exact cohomology sequence associated with the short exact sequence

        0 → μ_m → μ_n ──(x ↦ x^m)→ μ_{n/m} → 0 : H^1(μ_n) ──①→ H^1(μ_{n/m}) ──j→ H^2(μ_m) ──②→ H^2(μ_n).

To prove that ② is injective, it is enough to prove that ① is surjective. By Hilbert's Theorem 90, H^1(μ_n) = k^*/k^{*n}; ① is passage to the quotient

        k^*/k^{*m/n} → k^*/k^{*m/n},

and 3.3 follows.

Case 2: p ≠ 0 and Aut(E) is not reduced to ±1.

In this case, x is obtained by scalar extension from a point of M_H^o with values in a finite field (one has j = 0 or 2^6.3^3, and the field of definition of x is algebraic over the field generated by j(x)). We may therefore suppose that k is finite. Since Gal(k̄/k) = ℤ̂ and Aut(E,α) is finite, the Giraud H^2 in which the obstruction lies vanishes, and 3.2 follows. In other words, let x ∈ M_H^o(𝔽_q); there is a finite extension 𝔽_{q^n} of 𝔽_q and a pair (E,α) over 𝔽_{q^n} that defines x. The curve (E,α) is geometrically isomorphic to its conjugates under Gal(𝔽_{q^n}/𝔽_q). After replacing 𝔽_{q^n} by an extension, we may therefore suppose that there is an isomorphism

        φ′ : (E,α)^(q) ⟶̃ (E,α).

This isomorphism defines descent data from 𝔽_{q^n} to 𝔽_q if and only if the nth power of φ : E —Fr→ E^(q) —φ′→ E is the Frobenius endomorphism F of E/𝔽_{q^n}. In general, φ^n = Fβ, where β has finite order m. Thus φ^{nm} = F^m, and after extending scalars to 𝔽_{q^{nm}}, φ′ defines descent data from 𝔽_{q^{nm}} to 𝔽_q for (E,α). The descended curve solves the problem.

4. Numerical remarks

We propose to translate into the language of algebraic stacks the classical formulas giving the genera of modular curves. To do so, we must first define the Euler--Poincaré characteristic χ(𝒞) of an algebraic stack of finite presentation over ℂ. This notion is related to Wall's virtual Euler--Poincaré characteristic of a discrete group.

4.1. a) Let (𝒵_i) be a finite partition of 𝒞 into separated locally closed substacks such that, over 𝒵_i, the group scheme of automorphisms of the objects classified by 𝒞 is locally constant of rank u_i. In other words, for every geometric point x → 𝒵_i, we require |Aut(x)| = u_i. Such a decomposition exists.

b) Let F_i be the coarse moduli scheme of 𝒵_i, and let χ(F_i) be the Euler--Poincaré characteristic of the topological space F_i(ℂ). Set

        χ(𝒞) =₍dfn₎ Σ (1/u_i) χ(F_i(ℂ)).

One checks that this definition is independent of the decomposition (𝒵_i). It agrees with the usual definition when 𝒞 "is" a scheme.

The Euler--Poincaré characteristic has the following properties:

α) additivity: if 𝒵 is a closed substack of 𝒞 with open complement 𝒰,

        χ(𝒞) = χ(𝒰) + χ(𝒵);

if 𝒰 and 𝒱 are two open substacks,

        χ(𝒰 ∪ 𝒱) + χ(𝒰 ∩ 𝒱) = χ(𝒰) + χ(𝒱).

β) multiplicativity: if f : 𝒞 → 𝒟 is a morphism and the geometric fibers 𝒞_s of f have constant Euler--Poincaré characteristic, then

        χ(𝒞) = χ(𝒟).χ(𝒞_s).

γ) algebraic character: the definition extends readily and makes it possible to define χ(𝒞) for an algebraic stack 𝒞 of finite presentation over an algebraically closed field k of characteristic zero.

δ) Let f : 𝒞 → 𝒟 be a finite flat morphism (i.e. flat, proper, with finite fibers), and let s be a geometric point of 𝒟. For a geometric point x of 𝒞_s, let Ã_x be the local ring of 𝒞_s at x. It is an Artinian ring. Set

(4.1.1)        deg_s(f) = Σ_x (1/|Aut(x)|) dim_{k(s)}(A_x).

This number is locally constant in s. If it is constant, denote it by deg(f). If f is finite étale, then χ(𝒞_s) = deg_s(f), and β) gives

(4.1.2)        χ(𝒞) = deg(f) χ(𝒟).

More concretely, a closed geometric point s of 𝒟 is simply an object of 𝒟 over ℂ, and a geometric point of 𝒞_s is an object x of 𝒞 equipped with an isomorphism α : f(x) ↔ s. One has

(4.1.3)        χ(𝒞_s) = Σ 1/Aut(x,α).

VII. The Tate curve.

In §1 of this chapter, we use a method due to Raynaud to construct the Tate curve 𝔾_m/q^ℤ over ℤ[[q]]. This enables us to give an explicit description of the formal completion of 𝓜_H along infinity (§2). In §§3 and 4, we deduce integrality theorems for the coefficients of the Fourier-series expansions of modular forms.

1. Construction of the Tate curve over ℤ[[q]].

1.1. Let S be a scheme and t∈Γ(S,𝒪_S). We propose to construct over S a scheme Ḡ_m^t, isomorphic to 𝔾_m over S[t^{-1}], non-quasi-compact when t is not invertible, and from which generalized elliptic curves will be obtained by taking a quotient when t is nilpotent.

a) Let (x_i)_{i∈ℤ} be indeterminates. Ḡ_m^t is the union of the local charts (U_j)_{j∈1/2+ℤ}:

(1.1.1)        U_j = S[x_{j-1/2},y_{j+1/2}] /(x_{j-1/2}y_{j+1/2}-t).

b) Glue U_{i-1/2} and U_{i+1/2} so that their overlap is U_{i+1/2}[1/x_i]≃S[x_i,x_i^{-1}], with y_{i+1}=t x_i^{-1}, and also U_{i-1/2}[1/y_i]≃S[y_i,y_i^{-1}], with x_{i-1}=t y_i^{-1}; these opens are identified by x_i y_i=1.

c) No gluings other than those imposed by b) are made. If |j-j'|≥2, U_j∩U_{j'} lies over S[1/t]; over S[1/t], all the U_j are identified by

1.10. Let A be Noetherian, t∈A, and g a section of T_k over S=Spec(A). For every N define C_N=Ḡ_m^t/g^ℤ over A/(t^N). The C_N define the direct-limit formal scheme C over the completion of S along Spec(A/(t)). If A is t-adically complete, the formal generalized elliptic curve is algebraizable: the formal projective curve Ĉ is algebraizable by Grothendieck existence; for k=1 the identity section determines the law; in general fppf descent reduces to g=g_0^k and II 1.17 applies to the resulting covering.

The algebraization over Spec(A) is called a Tate curve and is again denoted Ḡ_m^t/g^ℤ.

Proposition 1.11. The image of the nonsmoothness subscheme of the Tate curve Ḡ_m^t/g^ℤ over Spec(A) is defined by t=0. It is the same image for the quotient, the formal scheme Ĉ, and the barred model.

1.12. For nilpotent t, the identity components of Ḡ_m^t and Ḡ_m^t/g^ℤ are canonically isomorphic to 𝔾_m. Hence the formal completion of 𝔾_m along its identity is isomorphic to the completion of the quotient; their Lie algebras are identified with 𝒪; and μ_n injects into the n-torsion.

For Noetherian t-complete A, formulas (1.12.1)--(1.12.3) give the corresponding formal-group isomorphism, Lie isomorphism, and inclusion μ_n↪(Ḡ_m^t/g^ℤ)_n. Tate curves therefore carry the canonical invariant differential dx/x.

4.5. Classically, a modular form of weight k and level n is a holomorphic function f on the Poincaré half-plane

X = {z | Im(z) > 0}

satisfying the following conditions.

(A) If (a b; c d) ∈ SL(2, ℤ) is congruent to (1 0; 0 1) mod n,

f(z) = (cz+d)⁻ᵏ f((az+b)/(cz+d)).

This condition implies that, for γ ∈ SL(2, ℤ/n), the image of γ₀ = (a b; c d) ∈ SL(2, ℤ), the function

f|γ₀ : z ↦ (cz+d)⁻ᵏ f((az+b)/(cz+d))

depends only on γ, not on the choice of γ₀. It is denoted f|γ.

(B) For every γ ∈ SL(2, ℤ/n),

(f|γ)(z) remains bounded as Im(z) → ∞

(it is equivalent, and more honest, to require f|γ to have polynomial growth in vertical strips as Im(z) → ∞).

Such a function is periodic with period n and therefore has a Fourier-series expansion

f(z) = ∑ aₘ e^(2πimz)    (m ∈ (1/n)ℤ, m ≥ 0).
translation_notes: The transformation law is kept in the authority's convention f(z)=(cz+d)^(-k)f(γz).
The lift γ₀ and residue-class element γ remain distinct.
The polynomial-growth parenthesis and the index set (1/n)ℤ with m≥0 are retained.

Construction 4.6. Modular forms of weight k and level n are identified with the sections

H⁰(𝓜ₙ ⊗_{ℤ[ζₙ]} ℂ, ω⊗ᵏ) = H⁰(𝓜ₙ, ω⊗ᵏ) ⊗_{ℤ[ζₙ]} ℂ.

Proof. Suppose first that n ≥ 3. In that case, 𝓜ₙ ⊗_{ℤ[ζₙ]} ℂ = Mₙ ⊗_{ℤ[ζₙ]} ℂ is a scheme. The analytic space underlying Mₙ° ⊗_{ℤ[ζₙ]} ℂ is

X/Ker(SL(2, ℤ) → SL(2, ℤ/n)),

and the holomorphic sections of ω⊗ᵏ on this space are identified with the holomorphic functions on X satisfying 4.5 (A). The analytic space underlying Mₙ ⊗_{ℤ[ζₙ]} ℂ is obtained from it by adding finitely many points. A holomorphic section of ω⊗ᵏ on Mₙ° ⊗_{ℤ[ζₙ]} ℂ extends to Mₙ ⊗_{ℤ[ζₙ]} ℂ if and only if it satisfies (B). By GAGA, these sections are the algebraic sections of ω⊗ᵏ on Mₙ ⊗_{ℤ[ζₙ]} ℂ.

The case of arbitrary n is reduced to the preceding one by passing to the invariants under

Ker(SL(2, ℤ/3n) → SL(2, ℤ/n))

in the space of modular forms of weight 3n. One could also invoke GAGA for the algebraic stack 𝓜ₙ ⊗_{ℤ[ζₙ]} ℂ.

4.7. For n ≥ 3, (Mₙ ⊗_{ℤ[ζₙ]} ℂ)ᵃⁿ is also the analytic space classifying generalized elliptic curves C/S over analytic spaces S, equipped with a level-n structure α such that det(α) = 1. From this point of view, a modular form f is a rule that assigns to every such curve a section of ω⊗ᵏ over S. The Fourier-series expansion is then obtained by evaluating the form on the Tate curve (4.3) (and multiplying the result by a power of 2πi depending on the normalizations chosen). For φ ∈ H⁰(Mₙ ⊗_{ℤ[ζₙ]} ℂ, ω⊗ᵏ), compatibility 4.4 shows that this expansion coincides with the expansion defined purely algebraically in § 3.
